blocks.how_it_works: A declaration of trust in Alaska is the written instrument that creates a trust under the Alaska Trust Administration statutes (Alaska Statutes Title 13, Chapter 36). The settlor states an intent to hold property for named beneficiaries and appoints a trustee to manage it. The trust is created when the settlor transfers property to another person as trustee, declares that the settlor holds identifiable property as trustee, or exercises a power of appointment in favor of a trustee. The instrument must be in writing and signed by the settlor. Alaska does not require witnesses or notarization for trust validity, though notarization is standard practice. Real property transferred to a trust must be recorded with the Alaska recorder. A successor trustee named in the document takes over if the acting trustee steps down, becomes incapacitated, or dies. When proof of the trust is needed, AS 13.36.079 lists what a certification of trust may contain, and a third party may require the trustee to furnish excerpts.

faq.q: Does an Alaska declaration of trust need to be notarized or witnessed?
faq.a: Under Alaska Trust Administration statutes, the trust instrument must be signed by the settlor. Witnesses are not required, and notarization is not required for the trust instrument itself. Notarization or an acknowledgment may still be required for recording purposes, such as real property transactions or a certificate of trust. Alaska also permits electronic records and signatures for trust matters, which streamlines the execution process for remote settlers.

faq.q: What makes Alaska's asset protection trust unique?
faq.a: Alaska was the first U.S. state to enact a Domestic Asset Protection Trust statute in 1997. Under AS 34.40.110-113, a settlor can create an irrevocable trust for their own benefit with spendthrift protection against creditors. The statute of limitations for fraudulent transfer claims is 4 years from transfer or 1 year from discovery, whichever is later. A qualified transfer affidavit must be sworn to by the settlor, stating the settlor has full right to transfer the property and does not intend to defraud creditors.

faq.q: What goes in a certification of trust under AS 13.36.079?
faq.a: The statute lists the contents: that the trust exists and the date the instrument was executed, the identity of the settlor, the identity and address of the currently acting trustee, the powers of the trustee, whether the trust is revocable and who holds the power to revoke, co-trustee signing authority, and the name in which title to trust property is held. The certification must also state that the trust has not been revoked, modified, or amended in a manner that would cause the representations to be incorrect.

faq.q: How long can an Alaska trust last?
faq.a: Alaska allows dynasty trusts to exist for up to 1,000 years under AS 34.27.051, measured from the date of trust creation, for both real and personal property. This is one of the longest dynasty trust periods in the nation. Alaska also has comprehensive directed trust statutes allowing separation of trustee powers with explicit liability protection, and broad decanting powers enacted in 2014.

blocks.common_mistakes: Common issues include assuming Alaska law requires witnesses or notarization for the trust instrument itself (it requires neither, though recording-related steps such as deeds or certificates of trust may call for an acknowledgment), and leaving the trust unfunded so that property never actually moves into it through a new deed or retitled accounts. Another frequent mix-up is treating a DAPT like a standard revocable trust; Alaska's self-settled asset protection trusts require an irrevocable structure and a qualified transfer affidavit. People also assume the certification of trust is the same as the trust instrument; under AS 13.36.079, a third party may require the complete trust instrument in addition to the certification, but bad-faith demands trigger civil penalties of up to $1,000 plus actual damages, court costs, and attorney fees.
blocks.state_notes: Alaska operates under Alaska Statutes Title 13, Chapter 36, and was the pioneering state for self-settled asset protection trusts in the United States. Certification of trust contents are set by AS 13.36.079, and a third party may require the trustee to furnish excerpts from the trust instrument. Alaska levies no state income tax, making it extremely favorable for trust income accumulation. The state has no state estate tax. Alaska allows dynasty trusts up to 1,000 years under AS 34.27.051. The state has comprehensive directed trust statutes (AS 13.36.370-375) and trust protector provisions (AS 13.36.390). Broad decanting powers under AS 13.36.157 allow trustees with discretionary distribution authority to distribute to new trusts with modified terms without court approval. Alaska's DAPT statute (AS 34.40.110-113) requires a 4-year statute of limitations for fraudulent transfer claims and a qualified transfer affidavit sworn by the settlor.
